name: Boost
summary: A large C++ library distribution organized as independently documented libraries, combining header-only components with separately built binaries and a portable Boost.Build integration path.

features.name: Modular library distribution
features.description: Boost organizes a broad set of libraries with public headers under boost/ and library-specific source, tests, and documentation under libs/, while the official library index describes them independently by function and category.
benefits: Allows consumers to adopt focused library components
Provides a common distribution and documentation structure for varied C++ facilities
costs: Library dependencies and support policies vary across the distribution
The broad surface increases discovery and compatibility coordination cost

features.name: Header-only and separately compiled components
features.description: The Boost getting-started documentation distinguishes libraries implemented entirely in headers from libraries that must be built separately, with some libraries offering optional binary components.
benefits: Header-only components can be consumed without a library build step
Compiled components can provide facilities that require separately built binaries
costs: Template-heavy headers can increase compile-time and configuration coupling
Binary components require matching toolset, threading, ABI, and build settings

features.name: Boost.Build toolset configuration
features.description: Boost documents Boost.Build as a text-based build system for developing, testing, and installing software, with toolset, variant, architecture, address-model, and build-directory options that shape generated binaries.
benefits: Provides a common build path across supported C++ toolsets
Makes important binary-compatibility choices explicit in build configuration
costs: The configuration space grows with toolsets, variants, platforms, and ABI options
Consumers must select binaries compatible with their application configuration

mathematical_views.question: How can a broad C++ distribution be decomposed into independently consumable libraries and their dependencies?
assumptions: Libraries are vertices and include, link, or build dependencies are directed edges
The graph distinguishes header-only consumption from separately compiled artifacts
The view abstracts template instantiation cost and platform-specific dependency resolution

mathematical_views.question: Under which toolset and ABI configurations can a generated Boost binary be linked into a consumer program?
assumptions: A binary is modeled with attributes such as toolset, threading, variant, architecture, and address model
A consumer and binary are compatible only when required configuration attributes agree
The relation is a candidate model and does not establish compatibility for every platform or library

benefits: Reuse across a wide range of C++ application domains
costs: Large and heterogeneous library surface increases selection and dependency complexity

benefits: Flexible choice between direct inclusion and prebuilt binary linkage
costs: Consumers must manage compile-time and binary-compatibility trade-offs
Toolset and ABI variation expands the build and test matrix
